newsitem.title: USA: TI sees global chip market growing 10 percent in 1997.
newsitem.headline: TI sees global chip market growing 10 percent in 1997.

text.p: Texas Instruments Inc. said on Thursday it expects the global semiconductor market to grow 10 percent in 1997 as it recovers from a disastrous collapse of memory chip prices last year.

The Dallas-based semiconductor giant said the global market should grow to $144 billion. That would make up for the ground lost last year, when the market dropped 9 percent as prices for the most common memory chips plunged about 80 percent.

TI said growth in 1997 and beyond would be spearheaded by high-tech products like digital signal processors, or DSPs, which translate sounds and sights into digital computer language. They are used in cellular telephones, modems, digital video and digital light processing.

Company officials said the DSPs market segment would grow in excess of 40 percent this year and that mixed-signal/analog chips would also grow strongly, helping compensate for continued weakness in memory chips.
Tom Engibous, TI's president and chief executive officer, told a conference of industry analysts that the company was banking its future on DSPs and other so-called differentiated semiconductors.
He said he was optimistic TI's strategy of recently divesting its defence-electronics and notebook computer business units to focus on new chip products would pay off.
"Firstly, DSPs is a great market and, secondly, TI has a great position in it," he said.

TI's chief economist, Vladi Catto, said this year's industry recovery is being fuelled by steady growth in electronic equipment as the personal computer market continues to grow at 15-20 percent per year, a sudden decline in customer inventories to "historically low levels" and lower capital spending by chip manufacturers.

He said an economic slowdown in Japan would hurt sales there but that firm economic growth in the United States, a slow recovery in Europe and rapid expansion in the Asia-Pacific region was helping business growth.
Catto said he expects the global chip market to grow at around 20 percent per year after 1997, reaching $330 billion by the year 2001.
"We are now on the threshold of a high-tech revolution that will last a very long time," said Catto, adding that the Internet would be a major catalyst for rapid long-term growth.
He said he expects the number of personal computers to almost quadruple to 12 for every 100 people in the world by the year 2010. In 1995, there were three computers for every 100 people.
Texas Instruments' stock was off $1.50 at $81.75 in midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
